clue.text: Victor is one getting on, showing imagination (6)

blocks.note: Victor is V in the NATO spelling alphabet
the word is taken straight, two letters as written
one is the Roman numeral I
another word lifted whole from the clue

explanation.surface: Victor, advancing in years, still comes up with imaginative ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: Victor is the NATO alphabet's V, the same list that hands out Romeo and Tango. The surface's 'getting on' means ageing; the parse wants only the ON.
explanation.definitionFit: A person of vision is one who imagines what is not yet there, so the noun stands in for imagination as a faculty.

clue.text: Very bad period for small community (7)

blocks.note: v. is the dictionary's short form of very
ill will and ill fortune are bad ones
an age is a stretch of time

explanation.surface: A rough patch endured by a little settlement.
explanation.walkthrough: V for 'very' is the abbreviation printed in dictionaries and on labels. The three pieces are plain; what hides them is that the seams fall inside syllables rather than between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A village is the smallest named settlement there is, a few hundred people with a church and not much else.

clue.text: Gets rid of containers for grain? (5)

blocks.note: the boss's verb: to dismiss an employee from the job
the coarse bags corn and flour are stored and carried in

explanation.surface: A firm clearing out the bins its grain was kept in.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that grain is only one of the things they might hold. Both halves are plurals, which is the check that they answer to the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: To sack a worker is to dismiss them, and a sack is the rough bag grain travels in — one a verb, the other the object behind it.

clue.text: Fellows in boat given a sermon surprisingly (7)

indicators.note: What happens surprisingly does not happen as expected, and letters that defy expectation do not stay in the order they were handed over.

blocks.note: seven letters of fodder, exactly the length wanted

explanation.surface: A boat crew unexpectedly finding themselves preached at.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters love a fodder phrase that already belongs to the picture, and a sermon in a boat is one. The definition describes the men by the job they are doing rather than naming them.
explanation.definitionFit: Oarsmen are the men pulling the oars, so 'fellows in boat' points at the crew by what they hold.

clue.text: Very beautiful young woman with police sergeant you spotted outside church (6)

indicators.note: To spot something outside a thing is to set it down around it, so the piece named goes on both sides of what follows.

blocks.note: PS is the British rank abbreviation for a police sergeant
ye is the old form of you
ch. is the standard short form of church

explanation.surface: A stunning girl noticed standing with a police sergeant by the church door.
explanation.walkthrough: The Greek myth supplies the woman: Cupid fell for a mortal princess so lovely that Venus grew jealous. Two capitals wrapped round two more, and the seams vanish completely.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Cupid story Psyche is the mortal princess whose beauty drew the goddess's envy, so the definition names her by her one famous quality.

clue.text: 18d and I wandering round old European region (7)

indicators.note: To wander round is to move about with no fixed course, and letters that do that end up somewhere other than where they started.

blocks.note: the answer to 18 down supplies six of the letters
the clue's own I makes the seventh

explanation.surface: A girl and the speaker drifting about somewhere in the old Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: A cross-reference like 18d is a fodder supplier: solve that clue first and the letters arrive ready-made. Silesia straddles today's Poland, Czechia and Germany, which is why no single country owns the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Silesia is a historical region on the upper Oder, carved up between modern states, so it survives as a name for an area rather than a country.

clue.text: Cute salon refashioned as diplomatic building (9)

indicators.note: To refashion something is to make it up again in a different shape, which is what happens to letters given a new arrangement.

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder, the full length of the answer

explanation.surface: A smart little hairdresser's done up to look like an embassy.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is handed over in plain sight, two ordinary words that carry no letters of their own beyond themselves. A consulate is the junior partner of an embassy, one per city rather than one per country.
explanation.definitionFit: A consulate is the office a country keeps in a foreign city to look after its own citizens and issue visas, staffed by diplomats.

clue.text: Always starts to expect severe test in mountain (7)

indicators.note: The start of a word is the letter it begins with, so each of the words that follow gives up only its first.

blocks.note: ever and always are the same word in different clothes
the opening letters of the three words in order

explanation.surface: Someone forever bracing for a brutal examination up in the hills.
explanation.walkthrough: An initials instruction sitting in the middle of a sentence is easy to read straight past, because 'starts to expect' is perfectly ordinary English. The severe test and the mountain belong to the same picture, which is the setter being kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Everest is the highest mountain on earth, named after a surveyor-general of India, and stands for 'mountain' the way Hoover stands for vacuum cleaner.

clue.text: A combination of notes said to bring agreement (6)

indicators.note: Something said is delivered by mouth, so what matters is how the words sound rather than how they are spelt.

blocks.note: notes sounded together make a chord, and the clue supplies the A in front of it

explanation.surface: A few notes struck together are enough to settle a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: Say the article and the noun as one breath and the ear cannot tell where the join falls. Writing it down puts a doubled C in the middle that the spoken version never asked for.
explanation.definitionFit: An accord is a formal agreement between parties — the word the papers use for a peace deal or a trade pact.

clue.text: You’d hope not to be shocked by this in the bedroom! (8,7)

definitions.text: You’d hope not to be shocked by this in the bedroom!

blocks.note: the surface offers the sense of being scandalised by what you find
the setter means shocked at the mains, and the bedroom holds one appliance that runs off it

explanation.surface: Something in the bedroom that you would rather not find shocking.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark is doing the winking. Take 'shocked' literally and the clue stops being about scandal and starts being about faulty wiring under the covers.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: the thing is wired to the mains and lies in the bed, so a shock from it is the risk you hope it never takes.

clue.text: Carriage that sounds ‘appealing to the eye’ (6)

indicators.note: What a thing sounds like is what the ear receives, so the words quoted are to be judged spoken and then spelt afresh.

blocks.note: handsome is what is pleasing to look at, and the cab is spelt without its D

explanation.surface: A vehicle whose name promises that it is good to look at.
explanation.walkthrough: Hansoms were the two-wheeled cabs of Victorian London, the driver perched up behind the passengers. The D in the spoken word is barely pronounced, which is what lets the two spellings share a sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A hansom is a light two-wheeled cab for hire, named after its designer, and it is the carriage crosswords reach for first.

clue.text: Hidden old boy’s no longer ill (8)

blocks.note: OB is the school register's abbreviation for an old boy
the possessive ending comes along and adds a letter of its own
someone no longer ill has been cured

explanation.surface: A former pupil who has finally got over his illness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hidden' opening a clue normally promises a word buried inside the letters; here it is only the definition, and nothing is buried at all. OB for old boy is worth filing away.
explanation.definitionFit: Something obscured has been covered over so it cannot be made out, which is what hidden says of it.

clue.text: Doomed loony didn’t see (8)

definitions.note: Destined covers any fixed fate, happy or not; 'doomed' picks out the unhappy end of that range, and the clue asks you to take it that way.

indicators.note: A loony behaves in no sensible order, and letters described that way are to be put in none either.

blocks.note: eight letters once the apostrophe drops out

explanation.surface: A madman marked for a bad end who never noticed it coming.
explanation.walkthrough: Contractions are fair fodder: the apostrophe simply vanishes and the letters carry straight on. 'Doomed' and the man who cannot see it are the same gloomy picture, which is what holds the surface together.
explanation.definitionFit: What is destined is settled in advance by fate, and when the fate settled on is a bad one the word for it is doomed.

clue.text: Go wrong with modern technology in Conservative district (9)

indicators.note: It puts what has come before it inside what comes after, so the earlier letters are swallowed rather than set alongside.

blocks.note: a Tory is a member of the British Conservative Party
to err is to go wrong, as in 'to err is human'
IT is information technology, the office word for computers

explanation.surface: A Conservative constituency where the new computer system keeps failing.
explanation.walkthrough: Four letters of party name split apart after a single T, which is the hardest kind of container to spot. IT for information technology has been standard in clues since the eighties.
explanation.definitionFit: A territory is a stretch of land treated as one unit — a sales rep's patch or an animal's ground — which is what district means here.

clue.text: Expects adult was suppressing sex appeal (6)

indicators.note: To suppress a thing is to hold it down out of sight, so the letters named after it end up buried inside.

blocks.note: A was the British film certificate for adult audiences
the word taken straight from the clue
it is the old word for sex appeal, as in an It girl

explanation.surface: A grown-up keeping a lid on how attractive they find someone.
explanation.walkthrough: IT for sex appeal goes back to Clara Bow, the It girl of the silent screen, and crosswords have never let go of it. The insertion splits 'was' between its A and its S, where the eye slides past.
explanation.definitionFit: To await something is to expect it and wait for it to arrive, so the two verbs swap into a sentence unchanged.

clue.text: Old city region Salvation Army goes round (6)

indicators.note: Something that goes round a thing encircles it, so the letters named first close on both sides of what follows.

blocks.note: SA is the Salvation Army, the Christian charity with the brass bands
a part of the country is a region of it

explanation.surface: The Salvation Army doing the rounds of an old city quarter.
explanation.walkthrough: Two letters wrapping four is a favourite shape, and SA is one of a handful of pairs setters use for it. Sparta was the rival of Athens, a state that trained its boys as soldiers from seven.
explanation.definitionFit: Sparta was the warrior city-state of ancient Greece, long ruined, which is what makes 'old city' fair rather than vague.

clue.text: Herald left on border (7)

indicators.note: In a down clue one thing rests on another, so the first piece is written above the second rather than after it.

blocks.note: port is the left-hand side of a ship as you face the bow
the border of a thing is where it ends

explanation.surface: A messenger who has gone off and left the frontier behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' as the nautical side rather than the past tense of leave is the whole difficulty, and a down clue's 'on' quietly stacks the pieces rather than joining them.
explanation.definitionFit: To portend is to be a sign of what is coming, which is exactly what 'herald' means when it is a verb rather than a person.

clue.text: River flooding a road makes one excited (7)

indicators.note: A river in flood spreads over whatever lies in its way, so its letters spill into the middle of the words beside it.

blocks.note: a, then RD, the short form used on street signs
the Ouse is an English river — there are several — and a crossword regular

explanation.surface: A river bursting its banks across a road and getting everyone worked up.
explanation.walkthrough: English rivers are a small club in crosswords and the Ouse is one of the most used, usually because its vowels are so convenient. Roads flooding is the British winter news story that makes the surface read as fact.
explanation.definitionFit: To be aroused is to be stirred up into excitement, and the past participle does duty as an adjective meaning just that.

clue.text: Knight with spear meeting fate (8)

blocks.note: a lance is the long spear a mounted knight carries
your lot is what fate has dealt you

explanation.surface: An armed knight riding towards whatever destiny has in store.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface and the answer describe the same man, which makes this a gift once the spear is read as the weapon's proper name. 'Lot' for fate survives in 'a hard lot' and in casting lots.
explanation.definitionFit: Lancelot is the foremost knight of Arthur's Round Table, the one who could beat all the others and then ruined it over Guinevere.

clue.text: Girl’s story about a ship (6)

indicators.note: To go about a thing is to pass round it, so the word named first closes on either side of what comes next.

blocks.note: a story told to deceive is a lie
the article taken straight from the clue
SS prefixes a ship's name, for steamship

explanation.surface: A girl spinning a yarn about a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' is the pivot: it reads as 'concerning' and works as 'surrounding'. SS in front of a name means steamship, which is why crosswords treat those two letters as a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: A lassie is a girl in Scottish and northern English usage, the counterpart of laddie.

clue.text: Closest home in which to house an army group (7)

indicators.note: To house something is to give it room within, so the pieces named next are lodged inside the word already found.

blocks.note: a nest is a bird's home
the indefinite article gives its own letter
RE is the Royal Engineers, the British Army's engineering corps

explanation.surface: A house with room enough to put up a party of soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: The container word is only four letters and is split after two, so nothing of it survives looking like itself. RE for the Royal Engineers is one of the few regiments setters use.
explanation.definitionFit: Nearest and closest are the same superlative: the one of several at the shortest distance from you.

clue.text: One catches wild animal in theatrical location (7)

indicators.note: To catch a thing is to trap it in your grasp, so what is caught sits inside the word that catches it.

blocks.note: the number written out, three letters as spoken
a stag is the male red deer, wild on the hill

explanation.surface: Somebody manages to catch a deer inside a theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild' looks like a shuffling instruction and is only describing the deer, which is the trap here. The number spelt out rather than reduced to a numeral is the other half of the disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor who is onstage is out on the boards in front of the audience, so the phrase names where in a theatre they are.

clue.text: Disloyal types having skill, about to start terrible riots (8)

indicators.note: Something turned about faces the other way, so those letters are read back to front.
Whatever starts comes first, so the piece just made is set at the front of what follows.
Terrible things are in a dreadful state, and letters in a dreadful state have lost their proper order.

blocks.note: art is skill, and it arrives turned round
five more letters, to be taken in a different order

explanation.surface: Disloyal men with a talent for it, on the point of stirring up dreadful riots.
explanation.walkthrough: Art for skill is the sense behind 'artful' and 'state of the art'. 'About' here means face the other way, not the RE of business letters — the other job that word does in clues.
explanation.definitionFit: Traitors betray the side they belong to, so 'disloyal types' names them by the fault rather than by the crime it amounts to.

clue.text: In the morning one George or another is lying in wait (6)

blocks.note: am marks the hours before noon
two American presidents were called George Bush, father and son, so either one answers

explanation.surface: Early in the day, one or other of the Georges is hiding and waiting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One George or another' is doing two jobs: it names the surname without naming the man, and it excuses the setter from choosing between them. Nothing is hidden or reversed — the two pieces simply sit side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: An ambush is a concealed lying in wait for someone to pass, so the definition describes the act the noun names.

clue.text: Liberty – sadly it is denied female (5)

indicators.note: What is done sadly is not done properly, and letters handled that way come out in some other order.
To be denied something is to have it withheld, so those letters never make it into what is being built.

blocks.note: the seven letters to work on
these two are withheld, leaving five to rearrange

explanation.surface: Freedom regrettably withheld from a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Liberty losing IT is the kind of quiet subtraction that only shows up once you count the letters. What survives the loss still has to be unsettled before it reads as a name.
explanation.definitionFit: Beryl is a woman's first name, common in Britain in the middle of the last century, so 'female' defines it by example.

clue.text: Discover man here being excited by this local dairy product (10,5)

indicators.note: Something excited will not sit still, and letters that will not sit still are to be stirred into another order.

blocks.note: fifteen letters of fodder, the full span of the grid row

explanation.surface: Finding a man who has got thoroughly worked up over the local speciality.
explanation.walkthrough: Devon is the county in south-west England whose thick clotted cream goes on scones with jam, and holidaymakers carry it home in pots. A fifteen-letter anagram looks daunting and is actually the friendliest kind, because the crossings pin it down fast.
explanation.definitionFit: Devonshire cream is the clotted cream made in Devon, so 'local dairy product' names it as the thing that county is known for producing.

clue.text: Fathers admitting right yen for alluring females (6)

indicators.note: To admit someone is to let them in through the door, so the letters admitted go inside the word doing the admitting.

blocks.note: dads are fathers, and the plural matters
R is the standard abbreviation for right
Y is the currency symbol for the Japanese yen

explanation.surface: Fathers letting through a proper claim for some Japanese money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yen' offers a longing and a currency, and only the currency pays. Two single letters going in together after the first D is what makes the short word so hard to see coming apart.
explanation.definitionFit: Dryads are the wood nymphs of Greek myth, female spirits living in the trees and famous for drawing mortals off the path.

clue.text: PM keeping dry in a shelter (6)

indicators.note: To keep a thing is to hold on to it inside, so one piece closes around the letters it keeps.

blocks.note: a, then LEE — the lee of a hill or a ship is its sheltered side, out of the wind
TT is teetotal, and a teetotaller takes no drink

explanation.surface: A prime minister staying out of the rain under cover.
explanation.walkthrough: Clement Attlee was the Labour leader who beat Churchill in 1945 and founded the National Health Service, and his double T is the reason setters keep reaching for him. Dry for teetotal is the pub sense, not the weather one the surface offers.
explanation.definitionFit: Attlee held the office outright from 1945 to 1951, so 'PM' defines him by the post he is remembered for.
